To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) EGFR is intrinsically active and contributes to KRASG12D-driven tumorigenesis and resistance to KRASG 12C inhibition; (2) KRASG12V and KRASG12A do not drive tumorigenesis or confer resistance to KRAS G12C inhibition; and (3) the combination of KRASG 1 2C inhibitors and EGFR inhibitors is a promising treatment strategy for KRASG12 D-driven tumors

(i) KRASG12CDN cells have high endogenous EGFER activity and are resistant to KRASG12Ci; (ii) KRASG120DN cells are sensitive to KRASG120Ci in the presence of anti-EGFR antibodies, but are resistant to KRASF120Ci alone; (iii) KRASG1210DN cells are resistant to both KRASG121Ci and anti-EGFR antibody treatment.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a novel approach for the treatment of colorectal cancer, which is based on the combination of a mutant-selective covalent inhibitor of the KRASG12 mutant and a small molecule inhibitor of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR).
the identification of novel therapeutic targets and the development of novel therapeutic strategies to improve treatment options for patients with advanced colorectal cancer.
the role of EGFR signaling in intrinsic resistance to KRASG12 inhibitors in CRC.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
KRASG12D and KRASG12V are oncogenic, whereas KRASG12S and KRASG13S are not.
KRASG12c inhibitors are active in patients with KRASG12D mutant colorectal cancer and that EGFR inhibition can be beneficial in patients who develop acquired resistance to KRASG12 inhibitors.
KRASG12CDN is an actionable target in lung adenocarcinoma, but not in colorectal cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the combination of KRASG13C inhibitor (AMG510) and cetuximab (anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody) has synergistic antitumor effects on KRASG12D colorectal cancer (CRC) cells, and that AMG510 is able to overcome cetuximab resistance in CRC cells.
the KRASG12D mutation in the colon is not the same as the KRASG 12D mutation in lung cancer.
we identified a novel mechanism of resistance to KRASG12D inhibitors in CRC.
The main takeaway from our work is that
EGFR is the key driver of resistance to KRASG12c inhibitor treatment in colorectal cancer, and that combination with anti-EGFR antibody therapy may be an effective strategy for overcoming resistance.
the KRASG12CDNAC inhibitor sotorasib (AMG510), which is now in clinical trials for the treatment of KRASG mutated colorectal cancer, may be ineffective in a subset of patients.
KRASG12c inhibition is a viable strategy for the treatment of colorectal cancer (CRC), provided that EGFR is inhibited as well.
